DRIVERS BECOMING HIS FRIENDS AND MORE FREQUENT GATHERINGS (2-3times a week), LATER INCREASED TO\u003C\/p\u003E\u003Cp\u003E260ml PER DAY OF WHISKEY\u003C\/p\u003E\u003Cp\u003EAROUND 2013 INCIDENTALLY\u003C\/p\u003E\u003Cp\u003EDIAGNOSED AS HYPERTENSIVE (ON tab AMLONG AT 5\/50)\u003C\/p\u003E\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cbr\u003E\u003C\/p\u003E\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cb\u003EHABIT TO hypertension is increased pressure within the portal venous system.\u0026nbsp;A pressure gradient of 6 mmHg or more between the\u0026nbsp;portal and hepatic veins (or inferior vena cava) suggests the presence of portal hypertension in most cases.When the pressure gradient is greater than 10 mmHg, portal hypertension becomes clinically significant. A pressure gradient between 5\u0026nbsp;to 9 mmHg usually reflects subclinical disease.\u0026nbsp;\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003ECirrhosis\u0026nbsp;of the liver is the most prevalent cause of portal hypertension\u0026nbsp;\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003E\u003Cbr\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003E\u003Cp\u003EComplications of portal hypertension include:\u003C\/p\u003E\u003Cul\u003E\u003Cli\u003EThrombocytopenia due to congestive hepatopathy\u003C\/li\u003E\u003Cli\u003EAbdominal wall collaterals\u003C\/li\u003E\u003Cli\u003EVariceal bleeding secondary to hemorrhage from gastroesophageal, anorectal, retroperitoneal, stomal, and other varices\u003C\/li\u003E\u003Cli\u003EAcute bleeding or iron deficiency anemia due to chronic blood loss from portal hypertensive gastropathy, enteropathy,\u0026nbsp;or coagulopathy\u003C\/li\u003E\u003Cli\u003EAscites\u003C\/li\u003E\u003Cli\u003ESpontaneous bacterial peritonitis\u003C\/li\u003E\u003Cli\u003EHepatic hydrothorax\u003C\/li\u003E\u003Cli\u003EHepatorenal syndrome\u003C\/li\u003E\u003Cli\u003EHepatic encephalopathy\u003C\/li\u003E\u003Cli\u003EHepatopulmonary syndrome\u003C\/li\u003E\u003Cli\u003EPortopulmonary hypertension\u003C\/li\u003E\u003Cli\u003ECirrhotic
